title: Pismis 24 (NIRCam image)
caption: The star cluster Pismis 24, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: constellation Scorpius · about 5500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI, A. Pagan (STScI)

recognition.text: Ranked #34 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A blue and black sky filled with stars of white, beige, yellow and light orange covers the top two thirds of this scene. Below rises a craggy, mountain-like landscape in orange, yellow and brown, with spire-like peaks and misty valleys, topped by a wispy white cloud. It looks like a starlit mountaintop, but it is really a landscape of dust being eaten away by the fierce winds and radiation of nearby massive young stars.

Those stars belong to Pismis 24, a young cluster at the heart of the nearby Lobster Nebula, some 5,500 light-years away in Scorpius. The region holds an active stellar nursery and is one of the closest sites where massive stars are being born.
That closeness makes Pismis 24 valuable. It gives rare insight into large, massive stars and is one of the best places to explore how hot young stars behave and evolve.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (4.22 x 5.83 arcminutes) and distance (5500 light years), the frame spans roughly 6.8 × 9.3 light-years. Its light set out about 5,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with one filter at the edge of visible light. The shortest wavelengths are shown in blue, then cyan and green, with PAH molecules in orange and molecular hydrogen in red.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the mountain's colours are a translation of wavelengths we cannot see.
